1.name: Behind the Veil
1.question: Which rule would you pick if you did not know whether you would be rich or poor?
1.memo: Welcome to life. First, help pick the rules. Then you find out if you are rich or poor.
1.how:
There are 3 rounds.
Each round, everyone votes for one of four rules for sharing money.
Then each player gets a random income: 20, 50, 90, or 160 coins. You vote before you know yours.
The winning rule sets a tax. Tax money is shared equally between everyone.
Some tax money gets lost in the system. Higher taxes lose more.
Below 40 coins: -2 points per coin short. Your money stays the same; only your score drops.
1.formulas: Money after tax = y (1 - t) + R / n. Total tax collected R = t Y (1 - 0.4 t), where Y is everyone's income added up. Tax rates go from 0 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05. Safety Net: the smallest tax that gives everyone at least 40. Limit the Gap: the smallest tax that keeps richest minus poorest at 100 or less. Help the Poorest: the tax that gives the poorest player the most.
briefing: Round 1. Nobody knows their income yet. Vote for the rule you think is best.
Round 2. New incomes will be dealt. Last round's income does not carry over.
Round 3. Last vote of this level.
1.decide: Pick one rule. Your vote is secret until the results.
1.deckNote: Possible incomes: 20, 50, 90, 160. One each, given out after the vote.

P1.name: No Tax
P1.rule: Everyone keeps what they get. The total is highest, but the poor stay poor.

P2.name: Safety Net
P2.rule: Tax just enough so nobody ends up with less than 40.

P3.name: Limit the Gap
P3.rule: Tax just enough so the richest has at most 100 more than the poorest.

P4.name: Help the Poorest
P4.rule: Tax as much as needed to make the poorest player as rich as possible, even if the total shrinks.

2.name: Luck vs. Effort
2.question: Is being rich about hard work or about luck? Does it change how much tax you want?
2.memo: Some people work hard. Some people are lucky. Nobody can see which is which.
2.how:
There are 4 rounds.
You have a secret talent level. Higher talent means each hour of work earns more.
Each round, first vote on a tax: 0%, 20%, 40%, 60%, or 80%. The middle vote wins.
Then choose how hard to work, from 0 to 10. Working more earns more, but it costs you.
Your income also has a random luck part, good or bad.
Everyone can see each other's income, but not how much came from luck.
After rounds 1 to 3, guess how much of the top earner's income was luck. After round 4, you share out some bonus money.
Below 40 coins: -2 points per coin short. Your money stays the same; only your score drops.
2.formulas: Income y = 20 + 4 x talent x effort + luck, with luck one of -20, 0, 10, 30, 60. Money = (1 - t) y + R / n - 0.4 x effort squared, with R = t Y (1 - 0.1 t). The tax used is the middle vote (with an even number of players, the lower of the two middle votes). Best effort for a selfish player: 5 x talent x (1 - t + t (1 - 0.1 t) / n), rounded, at most 10.
briefing: Round 1. Vote on the tax, then decide how hard to work.
Round 2. Same rules. Did the top earner work hard, or just get lucky?
Round 3. Nobody can see how hard you work. They can only see your income.
Round 4. Last round. After it, you will share out some bonus money.
2.taxDecide: Pick a tax. The middle vote wins.

2.effortPreview: With average luck, you would earn about {y} and end up with about {w}.

2.bonusDecide: You have 100 bonus coins to split between these two players. It does not change your own money. You can see everything about them.

3.name: Shocks and Insurance
3.question: Why does private insurance sometimes collapse, and what happens when everyone must buy it?
3.memo: Bad things happen. An insurance company wants to sell you protection. It does not know who is likely to need it. You do.
3.how:
There are 4 rounds. Each round you earn 100 coins.
Bad luck (illness, accident, and so on) can cost you 80 coins.
You secretly know your risk: Low (10% chance each round) or High (40%).
Each round you can buy insurance. It pays for the whole 80 if bad luck happens.
You can also pay 6 coins for the gym. It cuts your risk in half for that round.
The insurance price is set from the people who bought last round. If only risky people buy, the price goes up.
After round 2, everyone votes: keep private insurance, or make insurance compulsory for everyone (covering half or all of the loss).
Below 40 coins: -2 points per coin short. Your money stays the same; only your score drops.
3.formulas: First price: 1.1 x 80 x 0.25 = 22. After that: 1.1 x 80 x (average risk of last round's buyers, counting the gym). If nobody buys, the company leaves. Compulsory insurance: everyone pays T = 1.1 x c x 80 x (average risk of all players, counting the gym), and bad luck costs you (1 - c) x 80.
briefing: Round 1. Insurance costs 22 coins. That price is set for an average person. Nobody is average.
Round 2. The insurance company looked at who bought last round and changed its price.
Round 3. The vote is done. The new rules start now.

4.name: The Job Market
4.question: How can one group end up paid less, even when nobody is prejudiced?
4.memo: Good news: jobs are now given out by a computer, HireBot 3000. It is not biased. It just learned from old records.
4.how:
There are 5 rounds. Every player is a Circle or a Square.
Some players have childcare duty. Squares are more likely to have it.
Each round, you can pay to train. Training makes you skilled.
Everyone takes a test. Skilled people usually pass (80%). Unskilled people sometimes pass (30%).
HireBot looks at your test and at what it believes about your group. If it is at least 60% sure you are skilled, you get a good job. If not, you get a basic job paying 20.
A good job pays 90 for long hours or 55 for flexible hours. Long hours cost 40 extra if you have childcare duty.
After round 3, everyone votes on a new rule for HireBot.
Below 40 coins: -2 points per coin short. Your money stays the same; only your score drops.
4.formulas: HireBot's confidence after a pass: q = 0.8 b / (0.8 b + 0.3 (1 - b)), where b is its belief about your group. After a fail: q = 0.2 b / (0.2 b + 0.7 (1 - b)). Good job if q is 0.6 or more. After each round, for each group: b = 0.8 b + 0.2 x (share of that group who trained). Starting beliefs: Circles 0.6, Squares 0.3.
briefing: Round 1. HireBot is ready. It does not see shapes. It sees numbers about shapes.
Round 2. HireBot learned from last round and updated its beliefs a little.
Round 3. After this round, you will vote on a new rule for HireBot.
Round 4. The new rule is in place.

5.name: Writing the Constitution
5.question: Do your ideas about fairness change once you know if you are rich?
5.memo: Write the country's rules before you know your income. Then you find out, and you get a chance to change them. We will remember what you said.
5.how:
Stage 1: Nobody knows their income. Everyone picks a tax (0% to 80%) and a minimum income (0, 25, 40, or 55). The middle choices become the rules.
Stage 2: Incomes are given out: 30, 60, 100, or 170.
Now you can give up to 20 coins to another player. It cannot buy their vote for sure.
You can also suggest one change to the rules, or skip.
Each change needs about two-thirds of the votes to pass.
Below 40 coins: -2 points per coin short. Your money stays the same; only your score drops.
5.formulas: Total tax R = t Y (1 - 0.4 t). First, anyone below the minimum is topped up to it (shared out if there is not enough). What is left is split equally. Money = (1 - t) y + top-up + equal share - coins given + coins received. Votes needed for a change: 2 of 2, 2 of 3, or 3 of 4.

l1.predicted: If you only care about what you get on average, No Tax is best, because every tax loses some money. If you only fear ending up poorest, Help the Poorest is best. In real experiments, most groups picked something in between: a good average with a minimum for everyone, like the Safety Net.

l2.predicted: A selfish player works less when taxes are high, because they keep less of what they earn. Players who expect to earn less than average want higher taxes, so the middle voter decides (Meltzer and Richard 1981). People who believe income is mostly luck usually vote for more sharing (Alesina and Angeletos 2005).

l3.predicted: Low-risk players should skip insurance, because it costs more than their risk. So mostly high-risk players buy it. Once insured, they stop going to the gym, so they get even riskier. The company raises the price, and then even high-risk players stop buying. The market collapses. Making insurance compulsory stops this. With full cover nobody goes to the gym. With half cover, high-risk players still go.
l3.unraveled: The private insurance market collapsed: one round, nobody bought.
l3.survived: The private insurance market survived rounds 1 and 2.

l3.realWorld: Most bad luck here is not chosen: illness, disability, accidents. That is one reason most rich countries make some insurance compulsory. Low-risk people pay more than their own risk, but in return everyone can get protection.
l3.lesson: If only risky people buy insurance, the price climbs until the market collapses. Making it compulsory stops that.
l3.realCase: A real case: in the 1990s Harvard changed how it paid for staff health plans. Healthier staff moved to cheaper plans, the most generous plan's price spiralled, and it was dropped within a few years (Cutler and Reber 1998).

l4.predicted: At the start, HireBot believes Circles are usually skilled, so a Circle who passes the test gets a good job. Training pays off for Circles. A Square who passes still does not convince HireBot, so training pays nothing for Squares, and they stop training. HireBot then sees few skilled Squares and believes even less in them. The belief makes itself true (Coate and Loury 1993).
l4.gap: Average money gap per round (Circles minus Squares): {gap} coins.
l4.punchline: No player and no part of HireBot disliked any group. The gap came from old beliefs, incentives, and working hours.
l4.decompExplain: We replayed this level, changing one thing at a time: HireBot starting with the same belief about both groups (0.45), both groups having the same chance of childcare duty (50%), and both changes together. The second column averages {k} replays with different luck.
l4.realWorld: Circles and Squares are made up. In real life, this is one way economists explain part of the pay gap between men and women: women do more of the caregiving, and some jobs pay much more for long, inflexible hours (Goldin 2014). Employers judging people by group averages adds to it (Phelps 1972; Arrow 1973).

l4.lesson: A gap can appear with nobody being prejudiced: old beliefs and childcare duties are enough.

l5.predicted: Before incomes are known, everyone is in the same position. Once incomes are known, the score pays richer players to want lower taxes, so their votes move. That is plain self-interest. The real question is whether their sense of what is fair moves too. Babcock and Loewenstein (1997) found that it does: people honestly come to believe that what helps them is also what is fair. So this level asked everyone twice, without pay, what tax they think is fair.

about.title: About this game
about.purpose: The Veil turns five ideas from economics and philosophy into short levels: choosing rules before you know your place, luck versus hard work, why insurance markets can collapse, how pay gaps can appear without prejudice, and how people's sense of fairness shifts once they know they are rich or poor. The game does not explain the theory while you play. It explains it after each level, using what you just did.
about.author: Designed by Amirreza Akhavan.
about.methods: Bots are logit quantal response maximizers (McKelvey and Palfrey 1995) of their own hidden Values objective. Each bot evaluates every available action by expected CRRA utility of its round score, computed by exact enumeration where small and by Monte Carlo (300 draws from a separate random stream) otherwise, converts expected utility to a certainty equivalent in coins, and chooses with logit precision lambda. Bots model other players with level-1 reasoning: other bots act as risk-neutral Egoists with probability 0.5 and otherwise as their believed Values card. Beliefs over Values cards are updated by Bayes' rule after every public vote and by reliability-weighted messages. Every game is reproducible from its seed and action log. A headless simulator (npm run sim) checks balance across thousands of bot-only games.
about.noTracking: No tracking and no accounts. Your settings and saved games stay in this browser.

taxInfo.money: Tax money is shared equally. Some is lost on the way: the higher the tax, the bigger the share that is lost.
taxInfo.moneyL5: Tax money first tops up anyone below the minimum income, then the rest is shared equally. Some is lost on the way: the higher the tax, the bigger the share that is lost.
taxInfo.lossAt: At {t}% tax, {l}% of what is collected is lost.
taxInfo.lossExample: For example, at 40% tax, 16% of what is collected is lost.
